ingredients.name: butter
ingredients.original: 40 g butter, melted, plus extra for frying

ingredients.name: lingonberry or strawberry jam
ingredients.original: 2 dl lingonberry or strawberry jam, to serve

ingredients.name: heavy cream
ingredients.original: 2 dl heavy cream, whipped, to serve (optional)

steps.text: Whisk the flour and salt with half the milk to a smooth, thick batter.
steps.critical: Adding the milk in two parts prevents lumps.

steps.text: Whisk in the rest of the milk, then the eggs and melted butter.
Let the batter rest so the flour hydrates.
Heat a pan with a little butter. Pour in a thin layer of batter, tilt to cover, and fry until the edge lifts, then flip and fry the other side briefly.
Serve rolled or folded with jam and whipped cream.

notes.techniques: The batter is thin, like crêpe batter, and is spread by tilting the pan. Butter in the batter means the pan needs only a little extra fat.
notes.chemistry: Resting lets the starch absorb liquid and lets gluten relax, so the pancakes are tender and less likely to tear.
notes.variations: These are the everyday stovetop pancakes. The oven version (ugnspannkaka) uses the same kind of batter baked thick in a tin, often with bacon.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 225 °C. Put the butter in the roasting tin and heat it in the oven until melted.
Fry the bacon until golden and drain off most of the fat.
Whisk the flour and salt with half the milk until smooth, then whisk in the rest of the milk and the eggs.
Pour the batter into the hot buttered tin and scatter the bacon over.
Bake until puffed, set and golden brown.
steps.critical: Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes or it will not set evenly.

steps.text: Cut into squares and serve warm with lingonberry jam.

notes.techniques: Pouring the batter into a preheated buttered tin gives crisp edges, like a large Yorkshire pudding with a custardy middle.
notes.chemistry: Steam from the milk puffs the batter while egg proteins set around it; it sinks a little as it cools.
notes.variations: Baked as one sheet rather than fried one by one, so it is hands-off. Bacon makes it a savoury main, though plain or apple versions also exist.
